title: The Well That Moved in the Night
summary: A cunning landlord secretly moves boundary stones to claim a neighbor's stone well. Birbal uses ancient roots and compass measurement to expose the theft.
full_text:
In a village bordering the imperial highway, two neighbors, Manohar and Ratan, owned adjoining agricultural plots. In the corner of Manohar's land stood a valuable stone well that provided clear, sweet water even during dry seasons.

One morning, Manohar woke to find that the boundary hedge and marker stones had been shifted twenty feet to the west during the night, placing the stone well inside Ratan's property!

Ratan brazenly claimed: 'The well has always been on my land! The boundary stones were washed away by last week's rain, and I merely restored them to their ancient alignment!'

Manohar wept and pleaded, but Ratan had bribed the village patwari (record keeper) to forge a false survey map. In despair, Manohar traveled to Agra and petitioned Emperor Akbar.

Birbal was dispatched to the village to investigate the dispute.

Birbal walked the disputed border. Ratan pointed proudly to the newly planted boundary stones: 'See, Lord Birbal! The stones are straight and clear!'

Birbal looked at the soil, then knelt beside the stone well. He noticed an ancient, thick tamarind tree standing fifty paces to the north.

Birbal asked the village elders: 'How old is this tamarind tree?'

'It was planted fifty years ago by Manohar's grandfather, my lord.'

Birbal asked for a long measuring rope and the original village revenue ledger from the district archive in Agra, which recorded distances between natural landmarks rather than movable stones.

Birbal read aloud from the archive: 'The deed recorded forty years ago states: "The stone well sits exactly forty cubits due south of the trunk of the great tamarind tree."'

Birbal held the rope at the trunk of the tamarind tree and stretched it directly south to the center of the well. It measured exactly forty cubits!

Then Birbal stretched the rope to Ratan's newly planted boundary stones: 'According to Ratan's claim, this well should be sixty cubits from the tree! Unless Ratan wishes to claim that the fifty-year-old tamarind tree grew legs and walked twenty feet across the field during the night, the well belongs indisputably to Manohar!'

The crowd cheered. Caught by the unmoving testimony of the ancient tree, the dishonest neighbor confessed his midnight forgery.

Birbal ordered the boundary restored, fined Ratan fifty gold coins, and dismissed the corrupt record keeper. Akbar praised Birbal for letting nature's landmarks defeat human deceit.
moral: Truth does not shift like sand; fraudulent claims collapse under the scrutiny of measurement.
